newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Benign Irish CPI data sparks bond rally - brokers.
newsitem.headline: Benign Irish CPI data sparks bond rally - brokers.

text.p: Better-than-expected Irish consumer price index data triggered a rally in bonds with shorter dated stocks outperforming, Riada stockbrokers said on Tuesday.
The January CPI, the first monthly Irish CPI index to be published, showed a 0.5 percent drop on November 1996 and rose 0.9 percent in the 11 months since February last year.
This was well below market forecasts which had anticipated a 0.1 to 0.3 percent rise on November and a 1.7 to 1.8 percent increase on February.
By 1446 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was up 37 pence to 103.43 to yield 5.63 percent while the 8.0 percent Treasury bond added 38 pence to 111.49, to yield 6.35 percent.
Riada said in a note that the January sales impact probably swamped the number, but as there is no data available for January 1996 it is difficult to be precise.
Up until now the CSO has published CPI data on a quarterly basis so there are no monthly comparable readings for 1996.
"At first glance these latest inflation figures look positive," Bloxham economist Alan McQuaid said in a note.
McQuaid also warned that it would be dangerous to read too much into the numbers without corresponding monthly data.

McQuaid said prices of clothing and footwear, which showed significant price reductions, could be put down entirely to the January sales and it was quite likely these reductions would be reversed in February.
Riada agreed the key factor in the inflation number was the 8.3 percent fall in clothing and footwear prices, "... which has a six percent weight, so knocking 0.5 percent off the index".
Even allowing for this Riada estimates the underlying rise in the index at 0.1 percent which it said, if accurate, suggests a reasonably good performance.

Bloxham's McQuaid said although the government will be delighted with the CPI outturn the central bank, which is publishing its monetary policy statement at 1630 GMT, may still sound a word of warning about getting too carried away on low CPI numbers.

Ireland economic growth is estimated at around six percent in 1997 and Ireland's central bank has shown concern over the possibility of increasing inflationary pressures, particularly after the government unveiled an expansionary budget at the end of January.
Riada, which expects the annual 1997 inflation number to average 2.4 percent, said the low CPI numbers further confuses the issue for the central bank.

"This is remarkably low (CPI number) for an economy growing at the pace Ireland is and clouds the issue for the central bank: fiscal policy is expansionary, the currency is down against sterling, but the actual inflation data seems benign," Riada said.
